content: Measles is a disease caused by a highly contagious virus. Individuals infected with measles can transmit the virus through the air when they cough, sneeze, or even breathe. Symptoms of measles include a high fever, cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes, and a characteristic rash. Koplik spots, which are tiny white spots that appear inside the mouth, may develop 2 to 3 days after the onset of symptoms. In some cases, individuals with measles may develop severe complications, such as pneumonia, a serious lung infection. Although rare, severe cases of measles can lead to brain swelling (encephalitis) and even death. Measles tends to be particularly severe in infants, malnourished individuals, and those with weakened immune systems. Anyone who has not been fully vaccinated against measles or has not previously had the disease is at risk of contracting it. Measles remains a common disease in many regions of the world, including Europe, the Middle East, Asia, the Pacific, and Africa. In the United States, most cases of measles occur among unvaccinated travelers who become infected while traveling internationally and subsequently spread the disease to unvaccinated individuals within the U.S. Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself and others from measles. The measles vaccine is part of the routine vaccination schedule for children in the United States and is typically administered in two doses. The first dose is recommended for children between 12 and 15 months of age, and the second dose is given between 4 and 6 years of age. The measles vaccine is often combined with vaccines for mumps and rubella (MMR vaccine) or mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV vaccine). If you were born in or after 1957 and have never had measles or been vaccinated against it, you should receive two doses of the MMR vaccine before traveling. The second dose should be administered at least 28 days after the first dose. Individuals born before 1957 were likely exposed to measles during childhood and generally do not require vaccination with the MMR vaccine. Infants aged 6 to 11 months who are traveling internationally should receive one dose of the MMR vaccine prior to travel. However, this dose does not count as part of the routine childhood vaccination series. Pregnant individuals should not receive the MMR vaccine. Any unvaccinated person should receive the MMR vaccine immediately after their pregnancy. It is also advised to avoid becoming pregnant for at least 4 weeks after receiving the MMR vaccine.
